concepts.name: Feature Creep
concepts.description: The tendency for products, systems, or ideas to become progressively more complex as additional features are added over time.

concepts.name: Visual Proverb
concepts.description: A physical object or visual reminder that communicates a core principle and reinforces decision making.

concepts.name: Memory Chunking
concepts.description: The process of organizing information into meaningful concepts that reduce cognitive load and improve recall.

problems.name: Feature overload
problems.description: Products become difficult to use because additional features accumulate and dilute the original purpose.

problems.name: Information exceeds memory capacity
problems.description: People struggle to remember information when it is presented as disconnected data rather than meaningful concepts.

insights.author: Chip Heath & Dan Heath
insights.title: Simplicity requires actively resisting feature creep
insights.what_it_says: Complexity accumulates naturally as people add features and capabilities. Preserving simplicity requires deliberate discipline and continuous prioritization.
insights.why_it_matters: Without resistance, products and ideas become overloaded and lose effectiveness.

examples_from_source.what_happened: Jeff Hawkins limited the Palm Pilot to four core functions and rejected additional features that threatened simplicity.
examples_from_source.why_it_matters: The product succeeded by focusing on a few tasks and performing them well.
examples_from_source.transferable_lesson: Define what something will not do as carefully as what it will do.

decision_rules.condition: When designing products, services, or systems.
decision_rules.action: Reject additions that weaken the core purpose.
decision_rules.rationale: Additional features often reduce overall usability and focus.

patterns.description: Protect a core purpose from gradual complexity.

warnings.warning: Adding features because there is available capacity.
warnings.consequence: The product becomes harder to use and less effective.
warnings.prevention: Evaluate additions against the core objective.

application_patterns.when_to_use: When developing products, processes, services, or strategies.
application_patterns.adaptation_notes: Applicable to product management, operations, and communication.

when_not_to_use: Situations where functionality gaps genuinely prevent success
tradeoffs: Simplicity improves usability but may reduce feature breadth.
insights.evidence: The Palm Pilot would do only four things, but it would do them well.

insights.author: Chip Heath & Dan Heath
insights.title: Visual reminders can reinforce strategic priorities
insights.what_it_says: Physical objects can serve as memorable symbols of a core idea and help teams make consistent decisions.
insights.why_it_matters: Visual reminders reinforce priorities more effectively than abstract instructions alone.

examples_from_source.what_happened: Jeff Hawkins carried a wooden block the size of the Palm Pilot and used it to challenge suggestions that added unnecessary features.
examples_from_source.why_it_matters: The block became a constant reminder of the product's commitment to simplicity.
examples_from_source.transferable_lesson: Create visible symbols that reinforce important principles.

decision_rules.action: Use physical symbols to reinforce the core principle.
decision_rules.rationale: Concrete reminders help people remember and apply priorities.

patterns.description: Use a physical object to represent a core idea.

application_patterns.when_to_use: When leading teams, designing products, or driving change.
application_patterns.adaptation_notes: Useful for leadership, product teams, and organizational culture.

when_not_to_use: Situations where priorities are already universally understood
tradeoffs: Symbols improve recall but may oversimplify complex considerations.
insights.evidence: The block of wood became a visual reminder to do a few things and do them well.

insights.author: Chip Heath & Dan Heath
insights.title: Meaningful concepts are easier to remember than raw data
insights.what_it_says: People remember information more easily when it is connected to existing concepts rather than presented as isolated facts.
insights.why_it_matters: Communication becomes more memorable when it links new information to familiar mental structures.

examples_from_source.example_name: JFK FBI NATO UPS NASA IRS exercise
examples_from_source.what_happened: Participants remembered more letters when they were grouped into recognizable concepts than when they appeared as random characters.
examples_from_source.why_it_matters: Meaning transforms disconnected data into memorable chunks.
examples_from_source.transferable_lesson: Connect information to existing knowledge whenever possible.

decision_rules.condition: When teaching or communicating complex information.
decision_rules.action: Organize facts around familiar ideas or categories.
decision_rules.rationale: People remember concepts more easily than isolated details.

steps: Connect it to a familiar concept

warnings.consequence: People remember less and learn more slowly.
warnings.prevention: Attach new information to existing mental models.

application_patterns.when_to_use: When teaching, training, writing, or presenting information.
application_patterns.adaptation_notes: Useful in education, onboarding, documentation, and content creation.

when_not_to_use: Situations requiring exact recall of raw data
tradeoffs: Chunking improves recall but may obscure lower-level details.
